title: Supplier Verification in India: A Practical Checklist for International Buyers
excerpt: A field-tested verification checklist for buyers evaluating Indian exporters—covering legal identity, capacity, quality systems, export track record, and red flags that should pause a purchase order.

contentMarkdown:
## Verification is not distrust—it is procurement hygiene

International buyers lose more money to unverified capability than to openly dishonest sellers. A factory can be real, polite, and still unable to hit your tolerance, volume, or document standard. Verification answers a narrower question than “Are they nice?” It asks: **Can this organisation produce what we specified, at the volume we need, with evidence we can defend to customs, customers, and our own finance team?**

This checklist is written for buyers evaluating Indian exporters remotely or with limited site time. Use it as a gate before tooling deposits, large advances, or annual volume commitments. Pair it with [supplier sourcing](/supplier-sourcing) discipline and [quality and compliance](/quality-compliance) planning rather than treating verification as a one-time PDF collection exercise.

## Layer 1 — Legal and commercial identity

Confirm you are contracting with the entity that actually controls production or export.

**Collect and cross-check:**

- Full legal name, registered address, and trading name if different
- Company identification as available through public registries (for example corporate filings via the Ministry of Corporate Affairs where applicable)
- GST registration details consistent with invoices you will receive
- Importer-Exporter Code (IEC) status for export shipments
- Bank details on letterhead matching the contracting entity (not a personal account “for convenience”)

**Red flags:**

- Pressure to pay a different company name than the one on the quotation
- Refusal to share basic registration identifiers
- Multiple unrelated bank beneficiaries for the same PO
- Quotation issued by a trading desk that cannot name the manufacturing site

Trading companies can be legitimate. The issue is opacity. If a trader is the seller, document who manufactures, who packs, and who signs quality releases.

## Layer 2 — Site and capacity reality

Ask for a plant profile that answers operational questions:

| Question | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Owned vs rented premises? | Continuity and investment signals |
| Number of production lines / shifts? | Volume realism |
| In-house vs outsourced processes? | Control of critical steps |
| Peak monthly output for your SKU family? | MOQ and lead-time honesty |
| Current utilisation? | Whether your order fits without chaos |

Video walkthroughs help, but they are easy to stage. Prefer live calls that move through raw material storage, in-process checks, packing, and finished goods. Ask to see work-in-progress for similar items, not only a showroom shelf.

If your volumes are material, plan an on-site visit or commission a third-party capability audit. Remote-only verification is a risk acceptance decision—make it consciously.

## Layer 3 — Quality system substance (not logo collection)

Certificates can be informative. They are not a substitute for process evidence.

**Request:**

- Incoming material checks for critical inputs
- In-process control points for your product type
- Final inspection criteria and AQL practice if used
- Calibration approach for key measuring equipment
- How non-conforming product is segregated and dispositioned
- Traceability: can they link a finished lot to input lots?

For food, feed, pharma ingredients, and cosmetics, ask which destination-market schemes they already operate under. For textiles, ask about fibre claims, restricted substance workflows, and lab partners. For engineered goods, ask for sample dimensional reports and material certificates from recent comparable orders.

ISO or industry certificates should match the site and scope you will use. A certificate for a different plant or product family does not travel automatically.

## Layer 4 — Export execution track record

A strong domestic manufacturer is not automatically a strong exporter. Probe:

- Destinations shipped in the last 12–24 months
- Typical document set they produce (invoice, packing list, transport document, certificates of origin where relevant)
- Experience with your Incoterm preference
- Who prepares HS classification suggestions vs who finalises with your broker
- History of inspections, claims, or container holds (ask calmly; evasion is data)

Review a redacted sample document set from a past shipment. Consistency of party names, weights, and descriptions across invoice, packing list, and bill of lading/air waybill is a practical competence test. See [Commercial Invoice, Packing List and Bill of Lading](/blogs/commercial-invoice-packing-list-bol) and [trade documentation](/trade-documentation).

## Layer 5 — Commercial behaviour under light stress

Verification includes how the supplier negotiates.

Healthy signs:

- Asks clarifying questions about specs before quoting
- Separates tooling, packaging, and testing costs instead of hiding them
- Explains MOQ with process reasons (see [MOQ in International Sourcing](/blogs/moq-international-sourcing))
- Accepts a defined inspection window
- Provides a written production plan for the pilot PO

Unhealthy signs:

- Price that is dramatically below a normalised market band without a process explanation
- Reluctance to put quality criteria in the PO or contract annex
- “Trust us, we export to Europe/US already” without any verifiable detail
- Urgency to take large advances before sample approval

## Layer 6 — References and soft intelligence

Ask for two export customer references in adjacent markets. Prepare specific questions:

1. On-time performance on the last three shipments
2. Defect or claim handling speed
3. Communication during delays
4. Whether packing matched the agreed standard

Also check trade fair history, association memberships, and—where available—independent audit databases relevant to your sector. Soft intelligence never replaces Layer 1–4; it corroborates them.

## Layer 7 — Pre-PO gate: what must be true before money moves

Before deposit or full PO release, require:

- [ ] Contracting entity verified and matches bank details
- [ ] Manufacturing site identified (even if seller is a trader)
- [ ] Written specification and acceptance criteria attached to the PO
- [ ] Sample / counter-sample approved against those criteria
- [ ] Inspection plan agreed (who, when, pass/fail rules)
- [ ] Incoterm, payment terms, and document list agreed
- [ ] Lead time stated from material readiness, not from PO date alone

If any box remains open, you are financing ambiguity. That can be acceptable for tiny trials; it is poor practice for inventory that must clear destination customs cleanly.

## How verification connects to ongoing control

Verification at onboarding reduces surprise. It does not eliminate the need for shipment-level controls. For bulk readiness checks, use [pre-shipment quality inspection](/blogs/pre-shipment-quality-inspection). For category programmes, keep a living supplier scorecard: quality escapes, document error rate, and schedule adherence.

Buyers building an India supply base often combine remote diligence with periodic site reviews. AITH’s [supplier sourcing](/supplier-sourcing) and [quality and compliance](/quality-compliance) workstreams follow that layered model—identity and capacity first, then process evidence, then shipment controls.

## Proportionate depth by order risk

Not every PO deserves the same diligence budget. A practical way to scale effort:

- **Trial under a modest value threshold:** Layers 1–3 plus sample approval; document a conscious waiver of deeper site audit.
- **First bulk order or tooling deposit:** Full Layers 1–7, including references and a sample document set.
- **Regulated or brand-critical categories:** Add third-party capability audit and lab method confirmation before tooling.
- **Ongoing programme:** Annual re-verification of legal identity, bank details, and site scope—plus scorecard triggers that force a revisit after quality or document failures.

Write the chosen depth into your internal approval note. Teams get into trouble when a large order inherits the diligence level of a sample buy because “we already know them.”

Also separate **seller risk** from **product risk**. A well-verified trader still needs process controls at the actual manufacturing site. A well-verified factory still needs destination-label checks if your market rules changed since their last shipment. Verification is multi-dimensional; a green light on identity does not auto-clear labelling or residue testing.

## Closing note for first-time India buyers

You do not need a forensic investigation for every small trial order. You do need a proportionate checklist that scales with deposit size, regulatory exposure, and brand risk. Start with identity and capacity, insist on specification clarity, and do not confuse a low quotation with a verified supply line. When the checklist is complete, sourcing conversations become commercial rather than hopeful—and that is where durable India programmes begin.

When you are ready to move from checklist to shortlist execution, prepare a clear brief ([sourcing brief guide](/blogs/prepare-sourcing-brief)) and [request a quote](/request-quote) with the verification outcomes attached so suppliers know the standard they are being measured against.
